| Anthropic / OpenAI paid API | Paid | Yes | Commercial API terms do not train on inputs by default; the paid fallback |

## Rule 2: forced tool call, never "reply in JSON"

Every provider above supports function calling. Force the model to call your one tool:

- OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama): `tools=[{"type":"function","function":{"name":..., "parameters": schema}}]` and `tool_choice={"type":"function","function":{"name":...}}`. The result arrives in `choices[0].message.tool_calls[0].function.arguments` as a **JSON string**. Parse it inside a try block.
- Anthropic: `tools=[{"name":..., "input_schema": schema}]`, `tool_choice={"type":"tool","name":...}`. The result is `content[i].input`, already an object.

Write the schema tight: `enum` for categories, `minimum`/`maximum` for scores, `maxLength` on strings, `maxItems` on arrays, `additionalProperties: false`. Example: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket-schema.json`.

## Rule 3: validate, then fall through

A 200 response with an off-schema payload is a failure. Validate the parsed result against the schema; if it fails, try the next provider.

## Rule 4: never the only path

Free tiers have no uptime promise and change limits without notice. Order the chain cheapest first and end with a paid provider you trust. An outage then costs a few cents, not a broken feature. Log which provider answered, so you can see the free share and notice when it drops to zero.

## Rule 5: "configured" means a valid-looking key

A variable set to `YOUR_KEY_HERE` is non-empty and useless. Gate on the provider's real key prefix (Groq `gsk_`, Anthropic API keys `sk-ant-api`, OpenRouter `sk-or-`, Gemini `AIza`) so a placeholder skips cleanly instead of sending a doomed request on every call.

## The bundled router (Python stdlib)

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/structured_router.py` implements all five rules. Copy it into your project (it is one file, no dependencies) or call it from the CLI.

See the route before spending anything:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/structured_router.py" \
  --schema "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket-schema.json" \
  --data-class private --plan
```

Example output:

```
SKIP ollama-local     qwen2.5:7b-instruct  (opt-in env ROUTER_USE_OLLAMA=1 not set)
TRY  groq             llama-3.3-70b-versatile  (key ok)
SKIP gemini-free      gemini-2.5-flash  (fails privacy bar for private data)
SKIP openrouter-free  meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free  (fails privacy bar for private data)
TRY  anthropic        claude-haiku-4-5  (key ok)
```

See the whole call path work with no keys, no network and no spend (forced tool call, schema validation, privacy bar, fall-through). Unset keys get a fake one with the right prefix, and every eligible provider answers with the JSON in the file:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/structured_router.py" \
  --schema "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket-schema.json" \
  --input "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket.txt" \
  --mock-response "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/mock.json"               # answered by groq (mock)
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/structured_router.py" \
  --schema "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket-schema.json" \
  --input "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket.txt" \
  --mock-response "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/mock-fallthrough.json"   # groq off-schema, falls through to anthropic
```

`mock-fallthrough.json` uses `{"per_provider": {"<name>": {...}}}`; a provider missing from it fails as a simulated outage. Mock mode proves the plumbing, not the model: run one real call before you ship.

Run it for real on synthetic input (needs a key; makes network calls):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/structured_router.py" \
  --schema "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket-schema.json" \
  --system "Classify this support ticket." \
  --input "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/ticket.txt" \
  --data-class private
```

In Python:

```python
from structured_router import call_structured, RouterError

try:
    data, provider = call_structured(
        system="Classify this support ticket.",
        user=ticket_text,
        tool_name="emit_ticket",
        schema=TICKET_SCHEMA,
        data_class="private",
    )
except RouterError as exc:
    # every provider failed: show a friendly error, log exc.attempts
    raise
```

Provider list: edit `DEFAULT_PROVIDERS`, or pass a JSON file (`--providers` or env `STRUCTURED_ROUTER_PROVIDERS`); example in `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/examples/providers.json`. Model names change; check each provider's model list. Override the defaults with `ROUTER_GROQ_MODEL`, `ROUTER_GEMINI_MODEL`, `ROUTER_OPENROUTER_MODEL`, `ROUTER_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, `ROUTER_OLLAMA_MODEL`.

### TypeScript / Next.js shape

Same pattern in two files: `lib/llm/groq.ts` (raw OpenAI-compatible call, `JSON.parse` on `arguments` in a try/catch, throws on any failure) and `lib/llm/structured.ts` (try the cheap provider, catch, call the paid one, validate both with `zod`). Call sites import only `structured.ts`, so switching providers is a one-file change.

## Gotchas

- **Two places for the key on a hosted app.** Set it in `.env.local` for dev AND in the host's env settings, then redeploy. Without the redeploy the live app keeps using the fallback forever, and nothing errors.
- **A stale exported variable shadows a fixed `.env`.** If the router says a key is a placeholder right after you fixed it, print the prefix from the same process: `python3 -c "import os; print(os.environ.get('GROQ_API_KEY','')[:4])"`.
- **Record the free path as $0 in cost logs, with a comment.** If the account later moves to pay-as-you-go, update it.
- **Do not test with real user data.** Use synthetic input until the privacy check is written down.

## Verify (before calling the integration done)

1. The key authenticates: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $GROQ_API_KEY"` prints `200`.
2. `--plan` shows the route you expect for `--data-class private` (no provider with `private_ok: false`).
3. One real call on synthetic input returns schema-valid JSON, and stderr names the provider.
4. Fallback works: run once with the cheap key set to `gsk_invalid`; the answer must come from the paid provider.
5. Spot-check 10 outputs by hand against what a person would answer. Format passing is not quality passing.

items.name: scale-10k
items.description: Audit a web app for launch at 10,000+ users and fix what will break first. Covers the app's own process model and state (in-memory state, single process, slow endpoints, double-submit duplicates), auth provider cost, database and connection pooling, sessions, rate limiting and bot protection, transactional email, privacy compliance, and monitoring, then produces a scorecard, a cost projection, and an ordered fix list. Use when the user says "scale to 10k", "prepare for launch", "production-ready", "handle more users", "will this survive a launch", or "what breaks at scale". Pass an area (app, auth, database, sessions, rate-limiting, email, compliance, infra), --audit-only, or --cost-estimate to narrow it.
items.body:
# scale-10k: take a hobby app to launch-ready

Arguments (`$ARGUMENTS`):

- empty: full audit, report, then fix with confirmation
- one area: `app`, `auth`, `database`, `sessions`, `rate-limiting`, `email`, `compliance`, `infra`
- `--audit-only`: report, change nothing
- `--cost-estimate`: only the monthly cost table

Rating scale used everywhere below: **READY**, **NEEDS WORK**, **CRITICAL** (will break or leak at scale).

## Step 1: audit (read-only)

Run the checks for each area. Cite the file and line for every finding so the user can verify it. Never skip 1h: the app's own code breaks at launch more often than any provider does, and the SaaS areas below cannot see it.

### 1a. Auth provider
- Detect the provider (same detection as the `add-auth` skill).
- Look up its pricing page TODAY and record: free MAU limit, price per MAU past it, and the date checked. Hosted auth providers differ by an order of magnitude at 10k MAU; some jump from free to an enterprise tier. Flag **CRITICAL** if the projected bill at 10k MAU exceeds the user's stated budget.
- OAuth providers configured? MFA available for admin accounts?

### 1b. Database
- SQLite file on a serverless host: **CRITICAL** (no concurrent writers, the file may not persist between invocations).
- Serverless functions (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare) talking to Postgres without a pooler: **CRITICAL**. Look for a pooler URL (Supabase pooler on port 6543, Neon `-pooler` host, PgBouncer) or a serverless driver.
- Free-tier database: record its storage, connection, and pause-on-idle limits.
- Indexes: users(email unique), sessions(user_id), sessions(expires_at), and every foreign key you filter on. In Prisma/Drizzle schemas, check for `@@index` / `index()` on those columns.
- N+1 queries in list pages (a query inside a loop or a `.map(async ...)`).

```bash
grep -rnE 'DATABASE_URL|pgbouncer|pooler|:6543' --include='*.ts' --include='*.js' --include='*.env.example' . 2>/dev/null | grep -v node_modules | head
grep -nE '@@index|@unique|index\(' prisma/schema.prisma src/**/schema.ts 2>/dev/null | head -30
```

### 1c. Sessions
- Tokens in `localStorage`: **CRITICAL** (readable by any XSS). Use HttpOnly cookies.
- Long-lived JWT with no refresh rotation: **NEEDS WORK** (aim for access tokens of 15 to 60 minutes and rotating refresh tokens).
- Database sessions with no cleanup of expired rows: **NEEDS WORK**.
- Cookie flags: `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` or stricter.

### 1d. Rate limiting and abuse
- Libraries: `@upstash/ratelimit`, `express-rate-limit`, `rate-limiter-flexible`, or platform rules (Cloudflare, Vercel Firewall).
- Sign-in, sign-up, password-reset, and any endpoint that calls a paid API (LLM, SMS, email) must be rate limited. Missing: **CRITICAL**. An unlimited endpoint that calls an LLM is a direct path to a surprise bill.
- Bot protection on sign-up (Cloudflare Turnstile, hCaptcha, reCAPTCHA).
- Account enumeration: sign-in and reset return the same message whether or not the email exists.

### 1e. Transactional email
- Provider present (Resend, Postmark, SendGrid, SES)? Missing: **NEEDS WORK** (needed for verification and password reset).
- SPF, DKIM, and DMARC set for the sending domain: `dig +short TXT <your-domain>` and `dig +short TXT _dmarc.<your-domain>`.
- Volume estimate: plan for 1 to 2 emails per user per month at 10k users.

### 1f. Privacy and compliance
- Data export for a user (GDPR Art. 20) and account deletion (Art. 17).
- Audit log of auth events (sign-in, sign-out, password change, role change, deletion).
- Privacy policy linked from sign-up; cookie consent if you serve the EU.
- If you handle student records, health data, or payments, name the regime (FERPA, HIPAA, PCI) and stop to ask before building; those are not a weekend fix.

### 1g. Infrastructure
- Hosting platform, and whether production env vars are set there (not only in `.env.local`).
- `.env*` gitignored (see `secrets-hygiene`).
- Error monitoring (Sentry or similar) and uptime monitoring on the main URL.
- Backups: does the database plan include point-in-time recovery, and has anyone restored from it once?

### 1h. App architecture and load
- **Process model and state.** State kept in memory (a module-level list or dict, an in-process cache or session store, `global` counters), or data written only to the local disk of a serverless or container host: **CRITICAL**. It is lost on every restart or deploy, and the app cannot run two instances (each would hold different data). Look for a store that is not a database, and for a single `node server.js` / `uvicorn` / `flask run` with no persistence behind it.
- **Measured latency, not guessed.** Start the app locally and fire about 50 concurrent requests at the main list endpoint and the main create endpoint; record p95. Over 1 s: **NEEDS WORK**; errors or timeouts under that load: **CRITICAL**. Name the slow cause (a synchronous LLM or HTTP call in the request, an N+1 query, no pagination).

  ```bash
  npx autocannon -c 50 -a 500 http://localhost:3000/api/items            # Node; prints latency percentiles
  hey -n 500 -c 50 http://localhost:3000/api/items                        # or: brew install hey
  ab -n 500 -c 50 http://localhost:3000/api/items                         # or: ApacheBench (Ubuntu: sudo apt install apache2-utils)
  ```
- **Double submit.** Every create endpoint (sign-up, order, post, payment) needs both halves: the button is disabled while the request is in flight, AND the server rejects a duplicate (an idempotency key, or a unique constraint on the natural key). Test it: send the same create twice at once and count rows. Two rows: **CRITICAL** for anything that charges money or sends email, **NEEDS WORK** otherwise.

  ```bash
  for i in 1 2; do curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/items -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"dup-test"}' & done; wait
  ```

## Step 2: report

```
Area             Rating       Finding (file:line)
App architecture CRITICAL     items kept in a module-level list, lost on restart (server/store.js:3); POST /api/items p95 2.4 s
Auth provider    READY        Clerk, free to 10k MAU (pricing checked 2026-01-15)
Database         CRITICAL     Postgres direct URL from serverless, no pooler (lib/db.ts:4)
Sessions         NEEDS WORK   ...
Rate limiting    CRITICAL     /api/generate calls an LLM with no limit (app/api/generate/route.ts:12)
Email            ...
Compliance       ...
Infrastructure   ...
```

Cost table, broken down by auth + database + email + hosting + cache, each line with its source:

```
Users     Auth   DB    Email  Hosting  Cache  Total/mo
current
1,000
5,000
10,000
50,000
```

Priority list: CRITICAL first (security risk or will break), then NEEDS WORK before 1k users, then nice-to-haves before 10k. Ask for confirmation before changing code.

## Step 3: fixes (implement in priority order, one commit per fix)

**Rate limiting (Upstash example).** `npm install @upstash/ratelimit @upstash/redis`, then:

```ts
// lib/rate-limit.ts
import { Ratelimit } from "@upstash/ratelimit";
import { Redis } from "@upstash/redis";
export const ratelimit = new Ratelimit({
  redis: Redis.fromEnv(),               // UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL, UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN
  limiter: Ratelimit.slidingWindow(10, "60 s"),
});
// in a route: const { success } = await ratelimit.limit(`signin:${ip}`); if (!success) return new Response("Too many requests", { status: 429 });
```

**App state and duplicates.** Move in-memory state into the database (or Redis for caches and rate-limit counters) so any instance can serve any request. Move slow work (LLM calls, emails, exports) out of the request into a queue or background job and return quickly. For double submit: disable the submit button while the request is in flight, and on the server add a unique constraint or accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and return the first result for a repeat.

**Connection pooling.** Supabase: switch the server connection string to the pooler URL. Neon: use the `-pooler` host or `@neondatabase/serverless`. Self-hosted Postgres: put PgBouncer in front.

**Session hardening.** Move tokens to HttpOnly cookies, add CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated form posts, add refresh rotation, and schedule a daily `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now()` (see the `scheduled-agents` skill for how to schedule it, or use the platform's cron).

**Bot protection.** Add Turnstile to sign-up and sign-in forms and verify the token on the server. Env: `NEXT_PUBLIC_TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY`, `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`.

**Email.** `npm install resend`; templates for verification, reset, welcome, and security alert; set SPF/DKIM/DMARC before the first real send.

**Roles.** Start with a `role` column (`admin`, `member`) and a server-side `requireRole("admin")` helper. Move to role and permission tables only when you have more than three roles.

**Compliance.** `GET /api/me/export` returns the user's data as JSON. `DELETE /api/me` soft-deletes with a grace period, then hard-deletes sessions and personal fields. An `audit_log(id, user_id, action, metadata, ip, user_agent, created_at)` table with an index on `(user_id, created_at)`.

**Monitoring.** Error tracking plus alerts on a spike in failed sign-ins, a spike in sign-ups, and rate-limit hits.

## Step 4: verify

1. Build passes and existing tests pass.
2. Rate limit actually fires: `for i in $(seq 1 15); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/<limited-route>; done` shows 429s after the limit.
3. Pooler in use: the production connection string host or port matches the pooler.
4. App architecture: data survives an app restart, the load test p95 is under 1 s, and two simultaneous identical creates make one row.
5. A deleted test account can no longer sign in, and its export endpoint returns 401.
6. Re-run Step 1 and show the before and after scorecard.

## Step 5: final report

Before/after scorecard, files changed, updated cost table, and a numbered list of manual steps (accounts to create, keys to paste into the hosting platform, DNS records, migrations to run). Link the OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet and the host's serverless database guidance.

items.name: scheduled-agents
items.description: Run Claude Code as an unattended job on a schedule (cron, macOS launchd, Linux systemd, Windows Task Scheduler, or GitHub Actions) and know when it silently stops. Covers headless `claude -p` auth, locks and timeouts, success-only heartbeats, a separate deadman check, alert verification, and the rule that background tasks die when a headless turn ends. Use when the user says "run this every morning", "schedule an agent", "cron job for claude", "run claude headless", "nightly agent", "automate this daily", "why did my scheduled job stop", or "my cron job runs but does nothing".
items.body:
# scheduled-agents: headless agents on a timer, with a deadman

A scheduled agent fails in two ways: loudly (it errors) and silently (it stops running, or runs and does nothing, and every dashboard stays green). This skill prevents both.

You MUST, for every job you set up:

1. Create TWO scheduler entries: the job AND its deadman check (Step 6). A job delivered without a scheduled deadman is not done.
2. Give the deadman an alert channel that works under the scheduler: `--webhook-file` (the URL in a `chmod 600` file) or a literal URL. Never `--webhook "$ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL"`: cron and launchd do not see variables from your shell profile, so it arrives empty.
3. Live-fire the deadman once (`--max-age 1s`) and see the alert arrive before you walk away.

Bundled tools (Python 3 stdlib). Copy both into your project so the schedule does not depend on where the skill is installed (`run_headless.py` imports `deadman.py` from its own folder): `mkdir -p scripts && cp "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/run_headless.py" "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/deadman.py" scripts/`.

- `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/run_headless.py`: runs one `claude -p` job with a lock, a hard timeout, a saved transcript, and a heartbeat written only on real success.
- `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/deadman.py`: `beat` writes a heartbeat; `check` alerts when the last success is too old.
- Templates in `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/`: `crontab.txt` (job and deadman lines), `launchd.plist` (job) plus `launchd-deadman.plist` (its deadman), `task-scheduler.ps1` (registers both tasks), `github-actions.yml`.

## Step 1: pick the primitive

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| A job while the laptop is off, or on a team repo | **GitHub Actions** `schedule` (template `github-actions.yml`) |
| macOS, user-level job | **launchd** LaunchAgent (template `launchd.plist`); cron also works but launchd runs missed jobs after sleep |
| Linux server | **cron** or a **systemd timer** (`OnCalendar=`, `Persistent=true`) |
| Windows | **Task Scheduler** (template `task-scheduler.ps1`) |
| Something to happen later in THIS interactive session only | the session's own loop or schedule tools; they die when the session ends, so never use them for a standing job |
| A one-time future date | a scheduler entry with an end date, or a calendar reminder; a chat promise is a dropped promise |

Write the **off condition** in the job's header comment: when should this job be deleted? A job with no off condition runs forever after anyone remembers why.

## Step 2: write the job as one foreground turn

Headless mode is one turn: `claude -p "<prompt>"` runs, prints a result, and exits.

**The rule: background work dies when the headless turn ends.** Anything the agent starts in the background (a background shell command, a dev server, a sub-task it plans to check later, a `sleep` it means to come back from) is killed or orphaned when the process exits, and nothing comes back to collect it. So the prompt must:

- do every step in the foreground and wait for it,
- write its output to a file (or open a PR, or post to a webhook) before it finishes,
- never say "I'll check back on this later"; there is no later.

If a job truly needs to wait for something, make the wait a second scheduled job, not a background task.

A good job prompt (`prompts/digest.md`):

```markdown
You are running unattended. No one will answer questions.
1. Read open issues labeled `needs-triage` with `gh issue list --label needs-triage --json number,title,body`.
2. For each, propose one label from: bug, feature, question, duplicate.
3. Write the result to reports/triage-$(date +%F).md as a table.
4. Do not start background processes. Do not edit source files.
Finish by printing one line: TRIAGED <count>.
```

Restrict what it can do with flags after `--`:

```bash
-- --max-turns 30 --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Write,Bash(gh issue list:*)"
```

Never give an unattended job `--dangerously-skip-permissions` on a machine with your personal files and logins. Grant the specific tools it needs.

## Step 3: auth that works without you

Interactive logins live in your desktop keychain, which cron and launchd often cannot read. For unattended runs:

```bash
claude setup-token      # prints a long-lived token for your subscription
```

Put it in the job's environment as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (a `chmod 600` env file sourced by the job, a CI secret, or a user environment variable on Windows). Or use an API key as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Do not put an OAuth token in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; they are different credentials. Never commit either (see `secrets-hygiene`).

Test auth in a scheduler-faithful environment before scheduling:

```bash
env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN="$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" \
  "$(command -v claude)" -p "Reply with the word ok" --output-format json --max-turns 1
```

## Step 4: wrap it with run_headless.py

```bash
python3 scripts/run_headless.py --name daily-digest --prompt-file prompts/digest.md \
  --workdir "$HOME/projects/<your-app>" --claude-bin "$(command -v claude)" --max-minutes 20 \
  -- --max-turns 30 --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Write"
```

It creates `<workdir>/.agent-jobs/` (add it to `.gitignore`) holding:

- `daily-digest.lock`: present while running; a second run exits 4 instead of overlapping
- `logs/daily-digest-<UTC stamp>.json`: the full JSON result
- `daily-digest.heartbeat.json`: rewritten only when claude exited 0, the result is not an error, and the result text is non-empty

Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 failed, 4 already running, 5 timed out, 6 claude not found.

## Step 5: schedule it (copy a template)

Generate BOTH entries, job and deadman, for the chosen scheduler; `crontab.txt` and `task-scheduler.ps1` already hold both, and launchd needs `launchd.plist` plus `launchd-deadman.plist`.

All templates use absolute paths. Schedulers run with a tiny `PATH`, no login shell and none of your exported variables, which is the most common reason a job "works when I run it" and fails on schedule.

- cron: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/crontab.txt`. `cd` into the project before anything relative; in POSIX `sh` a failed `. ./file` aborts the whole line.
- launchd: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/launchd.plist` and `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/launchd-deadman.plist`. `plutil -lint` both first; an unescaped `&` makes launchd ignore the file without an error. After changing `EnvironmentVariables`, `bootout` then `bootstrap`; `kickstart` does not re-read them.
- Windows: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/task-scheduler.ps1`. `-MultipleInstances IgnoreNew` is the overlap guard.
- GitHub Actions: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/github-actions.yml`. Times are UTC, runs can start late, and on public repos scheduled workflows are disabled after 60 days without activity.

Never schedule the same job in two systems (for example cron and launchd). It double-runs and the lock hides it.

## Step 6: add the deadman (the job is not done without it)

The deadman is a **separate** scheduled entry that checks the heartbeat's content timestamp:

```bash
# once: the alert URL in a file the scheduler can read (cron and launchd do not see your shell's env)
mkdir -p ~/.config/agent-alerts && printf '%s\n' 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/...' > ~/.config/agent-alerts/webhook.url
chmod 600 ~/.config/agent-alerts/webhook.url

python3 scripts/deadman.py check --name daily-digest \
  --file "$HOME/projects/<your-app>/.agent-jobs/daily-digest.heartbeat.json" \
  --max-age 26h --webhook-file "$HOME/.config/agent-alerts/webhook.url"
```

- `--max-age` is about one period plus slack (daily job: 26h; hourly job: 2h).
- It reads the `finished_at` written inside the file, not the file's modification time, which a copy or restore can refresh.
- It exits 3 and says so when the alert itself fails to deliver, and also when no channel is set (no `--webhook`, `--webhook-file` or `--alert-cmd`, or only an empty one): stderr says `NO ALERT CHANNEL`. An alert that was never delivered is not an alert.
- On every stale or missing check it also writes `<name>.DEADMAN-ALERT.txt` next to the heartbeat, and removes it on the next fresh check, so a failure leaves a trail on disk even when every channel is down.
- `--alert-cmd` runs any command with the text in `$DEADMAN_MESSAGE` (for example a mail or notification command); it counts as delivered only when the command exits 0.
- Run the deadman somewhere the job's failure cannot also take down: a different scheduler entry at minimum, a different machine or GitHub Actions if the job matters.

Guard rules:

1. **Log success conditionally.** "OK" only on exit 0 and a fresh artifact. `my-job; echo done` prints done after a crash.
2. **Live-fire the alarm once.** Point `--max-age 1s` at the heartbeat and watch the alert arrive before calling the guard done.
3. **Never send the alarm through the thing it watches.** A job that posts to Slack should not be the only path for "the Slack poster is down".

## Verify (all must hold before you walk away)

```bash
# 1. the job runs in a scheduler-faithful env and writes a heartbeat
env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin sh -c '<the exact line from your crontab>' ; echo "exit=$?"
cat "$HOME/projects/<your-app>/.agent-jobs/daily-digest.heartbeat.json"

# 2. the scheduler has it
crontab -l | grep daily-digest                       # cron: expect TWO lines, job and deadman
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.example.daily-digest | head -5           # launchd: the job
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.example.daily-digest-deadman | head -5   # launchd: its deadman
# Windows: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName daily-digest ; GitHub: Actions tab, run once with "Run workflow"

# 3. the deadman fires: expect exit 1 and an alert that actually arrives
python3 scripts/deadman.py check --file .agent-jobs/daily-digest.heartbeat.json --max-age 1s --webhook-file ~/.config/agent-alerts/webhook.url
```

Then write the off condition in the job's header comment.

items.name: secrets-hygiene
items.description: Keep API keys and passwords out of git, scan a repo for keys before you commit or push, and rotate one correctly when it leaks. Sets up .env patterns, .gitignore, a gitleaks pre-commit hook and CI scan, then runs the probe-first rotation flow (probe the leaked key, map every consumer, mint new, swap all consumers, revoke old, re-probe until dead). Use when the user says "I committed my API key", "a key leaked", "GitHub sent a secret scanning alert", "rotate this key", "set up .env", "keep secrets out of git", "add gitleaks", "make sure I'm not leaking any keys", "am I about to commit a secret", "scan for API keys or secrets", "check for leaked credentials before I push", or before a repo goes public.
items.body:
# secrets-hygiene: prevent leaks, and handle the one that happens anyway

Two jobs. **Prevent** (set up once per repo, 10 minutes) and **respond** (when a key leaks). Do the response first if a key is already out.

Bundled tools (all Python 3 stdlib):

- `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/scan_secrets.py`: fallback secret scanner (`--staged`, `--worktree`, `--all`, or paths). `--all` covers tracked files AND untracked files that are not gitignored, which is everything `git add .` would stage. Redacted output.
- `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/probe_key.py`: asks a provider whether a key still authenticates (`LIVE`, `DEAD`, `ERR`).
- `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/commit_secret_guard.py`: the plugin hook (runs automatically only when this skill is installed as part of the foundry-builder-kit plugin). It blocks a `git commit` the agent runs when the commit would contain a secret: what is already staged plus whatever the same command stages first (`git add -A && git commit`, `git add <file> && git commit`, `git commit -am`). It reads chains, subshells, redirections, comments, heredocs, `cd`/`git -C`, runners like `timeout`/`xargs` and git aliases, and scans the command text too (a key in a commit message or in a file the command writes). Off for one session: `export FOUNDRY_COMMIT_SECRET_GUARD=0` in the terminal before you start `claude` (the old name `FOUNDRY_SECRETS_GUARD` still works; an `export` run by the agent does not reach the hook). The foundry-guardrails plugin's `FOUNDRY_SECRET_GUARD` is a different switch for a different hook.
- Templates in `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/`.

## Part 1: prevent

### 1. Where secrets live

| Value | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| Local dev secrets | `.env.local` (or `.env`), gitignored |
| The list of variable names | `.env.example`, committed, values empty |
| Production secrets | the hosting platform's env settings (Vercel, Netlify, Fly, Render), or a secret manager |
| CI secrets | GitHub Actions repository secrets, read as `${{ secrets.NAME }}` |
| Anything in the browser bundle | only values that are public by design (`NEXT_PUBLIC_*`, `VITE_*`). A secret with that prefix is published to every visitor. |

Code reads secrets by name (`process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY`, `os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]`). A literal key in source code is a leak waiting for a push.

### 2. Set it up

```bash
# from the repo root
cat "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/gitignore-secrets.txt" >> .gitignore
cp "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/env.example" .env.example   # then edit the names
git rm --cached .env .env.local 2>/dev/null   # stop tracking if they were committed (they stay on disk)
git check-ignore -v .env.local                 # must print the matching .gitignore rule
```

If `git rm --cached` removed a tracked env file, its contents are still in history. Go to Part 2 for every real key in it.

### 3. Scan before every commit (gitleaks)

Install gitleaks: `brew install gitleaks` (macOS), `winget install gitleaks` or `scoop install gitleaks` (Windows), or a release binary from github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks. Then pick one:

- **pre-commit framework:** copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/pre-commit-config.yaml` to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, then `pre-commit install`.
- **plain git hook** (copy BOTH files; `scripts/scan_secrets.py` is the hook's fallback when gitleaks is not installed, and without it the hook refuses every commit):

  ```bash
  mkdir -p scripts && cp "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/scan_secrets.py" scripts/ \
    && cp "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/pre-commit.sh" .git/hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
  ```

Scan what is already there, once:

```bash
gitleaks git --redact -v .            # full git history
gitleaks dir --redact -v .            # the files on disk, including untracked
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/scan_secrets.py" --all   # no gitleaks: tracked + untracked, skips gitignored
```

Add the CI scan so a teammate without the hook is still caught: copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/templates/secret-scan.yml` to `.github/workflows/secret-scan.yml`. Also turn on GitHub's own secret scanning and push protection (repo Settings, Code security).

### 4. False positives

Mark a line on purpose, and say why in the same comment:

```python
TEST_FIXTURE = "sk-test-not-a-real-key-000000000000"  # secrets-hygiene: allow (fake fixture)  gitleaks:allow
```

Or use a `.gitleaksignore` file with the finding fingerprints gitleaks prints.

### Acceptance check for Part 1

```bash
echo "OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-$(openssl rand -hex 24)" > leak-test.txt   # a random fake key, built at run time
git add leak-test.txt && git commit -m "should be blocked"; echo "exit=$?"   # expect a non-zero exit and a redacted finding
git restore --staged leak-test.txt && rm leak-test.txt
```

## Part 2: respond to a leak (probe first, rotate second)

A leaked key is any key that was ever committed (even if deleted in a later commit), pasted in a chat, issue, screenshot, or log, or sent to a model provider that retains data. Deleting the line does not un-leak it: `git show <old-commit>:path` still prints it, and bots scrape public GitHub within minutes.

### Step 1: probe liveness

```bash
export LEAKED_KEY='...'                     # paste into your own shell, not into a file
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/probe_key.py" openai:LEAKED_KEY
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/probe_key.py" --list   # supported providers
```

- `LIVE`: incident. Continue with Step 2 now.
- `DEAD`: the provider rejects it. Still scrub it (Step 6), but nobody can use it.
- `ERR`: unknown (network, 403, rate limit). **ERR is never an all-clear.** Retry, or check the provider dashboard by hand.

For a provider not in the list, the pattern is one cheap read-only GET with the key: 2xx means live, 401 means dead, anything else means unknown. Add it to `PROVIDERS` in `probe_key.py`.

### Step 2: map every consumer before you rotate

A key almost always lives in more than one place. List them all first, or the rotation breaks production.

```bash
PREFIX='sk-proj-ab'   # the first 10 or so characters, never the whole key
grep -rIl --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git "$PREFIX" . "$HOME"/.config 2>/dev/null
grep -l "$PREFIX" "$HOME"/.zshrc "$HOME"/.bashrc "$HOME"/.profile 2>/dev/null
crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -c "$PREFIX"
```

Also check by hand: the hosting platform's env settings, GitHub Actions secrets, teammates' machines, any scheduled job definitions (launchd plists, systemd units, Task Scheduler), and any app or script that copies config into a backup folder (it can re-introduce the old value later).

### Step 3: mint the new key, keep the old one alive for now

Create the new key in the provider dashboard. Both keys are valid during the swap, so nothing goes down.

### Step 4: swap every consumer in one pass

Update every location from Step 2 together. Then restart what caches env at start-up:

- dev server: restart it
- hosting platform: redeploy (Vercel and similar do not apply new env vars to an existing build)
- launchd: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label>` then `launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist` (`kickstart` does not re-read plist env)
- systemd: `systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user restart <unit>`

Smoke test each consumer with one real call.

### Step 5: revoke the old key, then prove it is dead

Revoke it in the dashboard, then re-run the probe with the OLD value. Done means `DEAD`, not "I clicked revoke":

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/probe_key.py" openai:LEAKED_KEY ; echo "exit=$?"   # expect DEAD and exit=0
```

If you cannot finish today, schedule the probe daily until it reports `DEAD` (see the `scheduled-agents` skill). The off condition is the probe result, never a note that says "rotated".

### Step 6: scrub history (only AFTER rotation)

Rotation is the fix; history scrubbing is cleanup. Order matters: scrub before rotating and you have spent time while the key still works.

```bash
git bundle create ../repo-backup.bundle --all && git bundle verify ../repo-backup.bundle
pipx install git-filter-repo
echo 'sk-proj-THE-OLD-KEY==>REDACTED' > ../replacements.txt
git filter-repo --replace-text ../replacements.txt
git push --force --all && git push --force --tags      # confirm with the team first: this rewrites history
```

Everyone with a clone must re-clone. Forks and cached copies keep the old history, which is why rotation comes first. Also scrub the key from issues, PR comments, chat logs, and notes.

## Gotchas

- Never print a full secret into a log, a chat, or a commit message. Use a prefix for searches.
- A JWT carries an `iat` (issued at) claim; decode it to prove whether a key was really re-issued.
- A stale exported variable in a shell profile or a long-running process shadows a corrected `.env`. Check the value in the same process that is failing (`python3 -c "import os; print(os.environ.get('NAME','')[:6])"`).
- An OAuth token and an API key are different credentials even from the same vendor; put each under the variable name the tool expects.

## Verify (all must hold)

1. `git check-ignore .env.local` prints the path.
2. The Part 1 acceptance check blocks the commit.
3. After a rotation: the old key probes `DEAD`, every consumer passes one real call, and a prefix search of the old key returns nothing outside backups you deliberately kept.

items.name: tmux-agents
items.description: Drive interactive CLIs and long-running processes from an agent through tmux. Start a REPL, dev server, database shell, SSH session, or another coding agent in a detached pane, type into it, wait for a prompt or a log line, read the output, and clean up. Includes running several coding agents in parallel in separate git worktrees. Use when the user says "run this in tmux", "keep the dev server running", "drive this REPL", "interactive prompt", "the command needs a TTY", "run several agents in parallel", "watch the logs while you work", or when a command hangs waiting for input.
items.body:
# tmux-agents: give the agent a terminal that stays open

Use tmux only when you need one of these:

- an **interactive** program (a REPL, `psql`, `ssh`, an installer that asks questions, another agent's TUI)
- a **long-running** process the agent must keep alive and check on while it works (a dev server, a watcher, a log tail)
- a session a **human can attach to** and watch

For a one-shot command that finishes on its own, just run it. tmux adds moving parts.

Bundled helper: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py` (Python 3 stdlib, calls `tmux`). Install tmux first: `brew install tmux` (macOS), `sudo apt install tmux` (Ubuntu/WSL). On Windows, use WSL.

Every command uses a **private socket, one per project** (the git top-level of the current directory), so the agent never types into the user's own tmux sessions, and agents in different projects never collide on a session name or kill each other's sessions. `T socket` prints the path. Run every `T` call for a set of sessions from inside the same project (in another repo you are on another socket; use `--cwd` to start a pane elsewhere). To share one socket on purpose (for example two terminals on the same sessions), export `TMUX_AGENT_SOCKET=/some/path.sock` in both.

The helper is a shell function, `T`. Define it at the top of every Bash command that uses it: a function does not survive into the next Bash tool call, and storing the command in a variable instead breaks in zsh, the macOS default shell, which does not word-split an unquoted variable into a command and its arguments.

## The five moves

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start dev --cwd "$PWD" --cmd "npm run dev"      # 1. start a named session, optionally launch a program
T wait dev "Local:.*http://localhost:\d+" --timeout 60   # 2. wait for a line (regex; --fixed for plain text)
T read dev --lines 50                              # 3. read recent output
T send dev "rs"                                    # 4. type text; Enter is sent separately
T keys dev C-c                                     #    or send control keys: C-c, C-d, Escape, Up, Tab
T kill dev                                         # 5. clean up (or: kill --all, this project's sessions only)
```

Run a shell command in a pane and get its output and exit code back:

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start sh --cwd "$PWD"
T run sh "pytest -q tests/test_api.py" --timeout 300 ; echo "exit=$?"
```

`run` wraps the command in unique begin and end markers, waits for the end marker, and returns the real exit code (124 on timeout, and the command keeps running so you can inspect or `keys sh C-c`).

After starting a session, tell the user how to watch it; `start` prints the exact line:

```
tmux -S <socket> attach -t dev      (detach with Ctrl-b then d)
```

## Rules that prevent the classic failures

1. **Wait for a signal, never sleep and hope.** `wait` for the prompt (`>>> `, `=# `, `\$ $`) or a log line before sending the next input. A fixed `sleep 5` is too long on a fast machine and too short on a loaded one.
2. **Send text and Enter separately** for full-screen apps (Claude Code, Codex, other TUIs). They can treat text and Enter that arrive together as a paste and not submit it. `send` already does this with a 0.3 s pause; raise `--delay` if submissions still get lost.
3. **Send literally.** `send` uses `send-keys -l`, so text like `C-c` or `Enter` inside your string is typed, not interpreted. Use `keys` for real control keys.
4. **Python REPL:** start it with `PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1 python3 -q`. The newer interactive REPL (3.13+) does auto-indent and paste handling that break typed input.
5. **Read with joined lines.** `read` uses `capture-pane -J`, which rejoins wrapped lines so a regex can match a long line.
6. **Clean up.** Kill every session you started before you finish. A forgotten dev server holds the port, and the next run fails with "address in use".
7. **Never type secrets into a pane.** Pane history is readable by anyone who can attach. Export them in the environment before `start`.

## Recipes

**Dev server plus tests against it**

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start web --cwd "$PWD" --cmd "npm run dev"
T wait web "ready|Local:" --timeout 90
curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/api/health
T start sh --cwd "$PWD"
T run sh "npx playwright test" --timeout 600
T kill web; T kill sh
```

**Database shell**

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start db --cmd 'psql "$DATABASE_URL"'
T wait db "=[#>] $" --timeout 20
T send db "\dt"
T wait db "=[#>] $" && T read db --lines 40
T send db "\q"
```

**An installer that asks questions**

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start setup --cwd "$PWD" --cmd "npx create-next-app@latest my-app"
T wait setup "TypeScript\?" --timeout 120 && T send setup "y"
T wait setup "ESLint\?" && T send setup "y"
```

(Many installers also accept flags such as `--yes` or `--ts`; prefer those when they exist.)

**Parallel coding agents in separate worktrees**

Each agent gets its own git worktree, so they never edit the same checkout:

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
for n in 1 2 3; do
  git worktree add "../<your-app>-task$n" -b "task$n"
  T start "agent$n" --cwd "../<your-app>-task$n" --cmd "claude"
done
T wait agent1 "for shortcuts|>" --timeout 60          # the TUI is ready; the pattern depends on the version
T send agent1 "Fix the failing test in tests/test_dates.py. Run the tests before you stop."
T send agent2 "Add input validation to app/api/signup/route.ts with tests."
T read agent1 --lines 80                              # check progress
```

Notes for parallel agents:

- Run the project's install step in each worktree before starting the agent.
- Detecting "done" from a TUI screen is fragile (prompt glyphs change between versions). For unattended work prefer headless mode, `claude -p "..." --output-format json`, and use tmux only for sessions a person will watch or steer.
- Two agents running the same dev server port collide. Give each worktree its own `PORT`.
- Remove worktrees after merging: `git worktree remove ../<your-app>-task1`.

## Raw tmux equivalents (when the helper is not available)

```bash
S="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-agent-$(id -u)-$(basename "$PWD").sock"   # one socket per project
tmux -S "$S" new-session -d -s dev -c "$PWD"
tmux -S "$S" send-keys -t dev:0.0 -l -- 'npm run dev' && sleep 0.3 && tmux -S "$S" send-keys -t dev:0.0 Enter
tmux -S "$S" capture-pane -p -J -t dev:0.0 -S -200
tmux -S "$S" send-keys -t dev:0.0 C-c
tmux -S "$S" kill-session -t dev
tmux -S "$S" list-sessions
```

## Verify

```bash
T() { python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/tmux_agent.py" "$@"; }
T start check --cmd "PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1 python3 -q"
T wait check ">>> " --timeout 10
T send check "print(6*7)"
T wait check "^42$" --timeout 10 && echo PASS
T kill check
T ls      # expect: (no sessions)
```

Credit: the send-text-then-Enter timing and the private-socket convention follow the tmux skill published by the OpenClaw project (MIT). The helper here is a fresh implementation.

items.name: commit-secret-guard
items.description: `skills/secrets-hygiene/scripts/commit_secret_guard.py`, wired in `hooks/hooks.json`. Blocks a `git commit` the agent runs when the commit would contain a secret: the index plus whatever the same command stages first (`git add -A && git commit`, `git commit -am`)
items.body:
### Commit secret guard (hook)

Enabled automatically with the plugin. It looks at every Bash command, ignores everything except `git commit`, and blocks the commit (with redacted findings) when what the commit WILL contain looks like a key: what is already staged, plus whatever the same command stages first. That covers `git add -A && git commit`, `git add . ; git commit`, `git add <file> && git commit`, `git add -f .env && git commit`, `git commit -a` / `-am` / `git commit <paths>`, and `git init && git add . && git commit`, across `&&`, `||`, `;`, pipes, newlines and subshells, with redirections (`2>/dev/null`, `2>&1 | tail`), `# comments` and heredocs read the way the shell reads them. It follows `cd`, `pushd`, `git -C DIR`, `bash -c '...'`, `eval`, runners such as `timeout`, `sudo`, `xargs` and `find -exec`, and git aliases (`git ci`, `!shell` aliases). A path known only at run time (`"$FILE"`, `$(...)`) counts as the whole tree. The command text is scanned too, so a key in a commit message, or in a file the same command writes with `echo` or a heredoc, is caught. The index is always scanned with the bundled scanner, and also with gitleaks when it is installed, so the verdict is the same whether a file was staged earlier or by this command; files the command is about to stage are scanned with the bundled scanner (untracked files over 2 MB are skipped, symlinks count as links, not as the file they point to). A command that copies a key in from outside the repo and commits it in the same call (`cp ~/key.pem . && git add . && git commit`) cannot be seen before it runs: the git pre-commit hook covers that. If the guard itself hits an error it lets the command run.

It guards commits the agent makes; install the git pre-commit hook from `secrets-hygiene` for the commits you type. Turn it off for a session by starting Claude Code with it off: `export FOUNDRY_COMMIT_SECRET_GUARD=0` in your terminal, then `claude` (an `export` the agent runs in its Bash tool does not reach the hook). The old name `FOUNDRY_SECRETS_GUARD=0` still works but is deprecated. Not the same switch as `FOUNDRY_SECRET_GUARD` (singular), which belongs to the foundry-guardrails plugin's secret-guard hook. Mark a deliberate fake with the comment `secrets-hygiene: allow` (or `gitleaks:allow`; each is honored by both scanners). Obvious placeholders (`sk-ant-your-key-here`, `ghp_xxxx...`, a value marked FAKE), AWS's documentation key `AKIA...EXAMPLE` and database URLs on `localhost` are not flagged.

### From the script header

```text
commit_secret_guard.py: Claude Code PreToolUse hook (matcher: Bash).

When the agent is about to run `git commit`, scan what that commit WILL contain and
block the command (exit 2) if it holds something that looks like a secret.

"What it will contain" is the current index PLUS everything the same Bash command
stages first, because agents usually stage and commit in one call:

  git add -A && git commit -m wip       tracked changes + untracked, not-ignored files
  git add . ; git commit -m x           the same, under the current directory
  git add settings.py && git commit     the named paths (quoted paths and globs work)
  git add -f .env && git commit         named paths, gitignored ones included
  git commit -a / -am / <paths>         tracked changes (whole tree, or the given paths)
  git init && git add . && git commit   the first commit of a new repo

The command is read the way the shell reads it: chains (&&, ||, ;, |, &, newlines),
subshells `( ... )`, redirections (`2>/dev/null`, `2>&1 | tail`), `# comments` and
heredoc bodies are handled; `cd`, `pushd`/`popd`, `git -C DIR`, `bash -c '...'`, `eval`,
runners such as `timeout`, `sudo`, `env`, `xargs` and `find -exec`, and git aliases
(`git ci`, `-c alias.x=...`, `!shell` aliases) are followed. A path the hook cannot know
in advance (`"$FILE"`, `$(...)`) is treated as the whole tree. The command text itself is
scanned too, so a key in a commit message or in a file the command writes is caught.

The index is always scanned with the bundled stdlib scanner, and also with gitleaks when
it is on PATH (more rules), so the verdict does not depend on whether a file was staged
earlier or by this command. Files the command is about to stage go through the bundled
scanner. Output is redacted. Any internal error lets the command run (fail open), so a
broken guard never blocks your work.

Turn it off: start Claude Code with FOUNDRY_COMMIT_SECRET_GUARD=0 in its environment
  (export it in your terminal before you run `claude`; an `export` inside the agent's
  Bash tool does not reach the hook). FOUNDRY_SECRETS_GUARD=0 still works; it is the
  old, deprecated name. The foundry-guardrails plugin has its own, different switch:
  FOUNDRY_SECRET_GUARD.
Allow a known false positive: add the comment  secrets-hygiene: allow  on that line
  (gitleaks:allow works too).

This guards commits the AGENT makes. Commits you type yourself need the git
pre-commit hook from the secrets-hygiene skill as well. A command that copies a secret
in from elsewhere and commits it in the same call (cp ~/key.pem . && git add . && git
commit) is not visible before it runs; the pre-commit hook catches that one.
```
